Stated Claim / Post Context:
Chicago Bears are a more complete team with Jeffery Simmons on board: Brad Biggs’ 10 thoughts on Week 8 win

On the night the Chicago Bears completed a two-game sweep of last year’s Super Bowl participants, defensive coordinator Dennis Allen reinvented the team on the fly. Brad Biggs’ 10 thoughts on the Week 8 win.

Actual Article Body:
eNewspaper

Sign up for email newsletters

Sign up for email newsletters

eNewspaper

Trending:

SEATTLE — On a night the Chicago Bears completed a two-game sweep of last season’s Super Bowl participants — they handled the defending AFC champion New England Patriots convincingly the previous time out — defensive coordinator Dennis Allen reinvented the team on the fly.

New defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons was every bit as good as the Bears could have hoped. In his first 10 snaps, he had a sack, a pressure of Seattle Seahawks quarterback Sam Darnold and three tackles. He finished tied with linebacker Devin Bush with a team-high six tackles and had two tackles for a loss and a pass breakup on his second-to-last snap.

“When I ran out of the tunnel, I kept telling myself: ‘It’s just football. Go out there and be me. Play by play, just stay in the moment,'” Simmons said. “That’s always my goal — just embrace the moment. That’s what happened tonight.”

10 thoughts on the Bears’ 34-17 win in Week 8.

Want the latest Bears news? Subscribe to the Chicago Tribune to read it all — and sign up for our Bears Insider newsletter.

It was a little more than 96 hours after Simmons arrived from Nashville, Tenn., in a blockbuster trade, the kind of calculating move Bears general manager Ryan Poles made with the Super Bowl — both this season and in coming years — in mind.

Simmons is slowly beginning to learn some of his new teammates. When he got to the sideline with only 2 minutes, 16 seconds remaining in the thorough beating of the defending Super Bowl champions in their home stadium, there were a few more handshakes and high-fives.

And soon Simmons found himself behind the bench, with a mass of Bears fans huddled near midfield in seats that the Seahawks faithful had vacated. He began waving his arms to the crowd, fans who believe he could be the missing link for a team that reached the divisional round last season.

Simmons played 55 of the 63 defensive snaps, more than any other lineman. The Bears got after Sam Darnold, and their three sacks and six QB hits don’t come close to painting the whole picture.

Nickel cornerback Kyler Gordon hit Darnold on a blitz on the second play. Simmons sacked Darnold on the first play of Seattle’s second possession, dominating right guard Grey Zabel. Devin Bush put a big hit on Darnold at the end of a third-down scramble on that possession, and the Seahawks quarterback rarely looked comfortable the rest of the game.

“At times, yeah,” Bush said when asked if he could sense Darnold was flustered. “I mean, yeah. Yeah! That’s what happens when you trade for a good player. We put him in the mix and stir it up, and it looks different.”

Darnold’s eyes started bouncing around as he scanned the field for targets. He was off target a couple of times to wide receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba. He had tight end A.J. Barner on a third-and-5 throw in the second quarter — one of the few instances the Seahawks didn’t face third-and-long — and missed. Darnold looked jumpy in the pocket against a four-man rush.

“Any quarterback, if you get pressure on him early and keep getting through, it’s going to make them rattled a little bit,” said James Lynch, whom the Bears have played at end and tackle. “That was our plan. I think we did pretty well. It’s fun to play like that.”

Darnold finished 17 of 34 for 188 yards, and the Bears rushed him with five or more on only 15.4% of his drop-backs. Through the first seven games — the pre-Simmons era — the Bears blitzed on 40.2% of opponent drop-backs, the fourth-highest rate in the league. That’s a massive drop-off for a defense that had to dial up pressures to disrupt quarterbacks through the first two months.

“They had a good plan,” Seahawks receiver Cooper Kupp said. “It was a mix of some stuff that we had seen but also playing a mixture of some (Cover-4), a few different two-man looks, did a good job with the safeties. They played it well off each other in terms of understanding the times that they can be aggressive at safety and be able to cut things and play low based on the pressure that they were generating or were expecting to generate.”

It all started up front — a critical element that has been missing for the Bears.

Lynch spent the last two seasons in Tennessee playing alongside Simmons. The journeyman was at home Thursday morning when he saw news of the trade on social media. Lynch texted his agent, Ron Slavin, because, well, some things that sound too good to be true often end up being … you know.

“Yep,” Slavin replied. “Deal went through.”

Lynch, 27, was gobsmacked.

“He’s just special,” Lynch said of Simmons. “I’ve been around a few players where it’s, ‘We can’t replace that.’ You can’t replace (Simmons). He wants to win. Hell of a player, but he’s a good leader. Does things the right way. Hustles and runs to the ball. He’s a good dude. I have played a lot of D-line and he’s by far — just in terms of everything that it’s about — he’s the best.”

That’s something the Bears said when explaining the trade that cost them first-round picks in 2027 and 2028. Simmons is more than a multiplying force in the middle of the defense. Those who have been around him say he’s the guy who shows others how to do it. Not every elite player is wired to also be a leader.

Simmons’ arrival sparked production from defensive end Montez Sweat, who had a sack and three hits on Darnold. Austin Booker tipped a pass into the air that Lynch intercepted, his first since high school.

The Seahawks had four three-and-punts, converted 1 of 11 third downs and, if you take out two modest scrambles by Darnold, had 17 rushes for 61 yards. Smith-Njigba got his customary 100 receiving yards (118), but nothing else worked for the Seahawks.

Center Garrett Bradbury joked that Poles should have traded three first-round picks for Simmons.

“I’d have given up every draft pick,” right guard Jonah Jackson said. “Give them the whole damn draft. I’m glad he’s on my team.”

Dennis Allen and the defense will continue to evolve. And there’s legitimate flexibility now if the Bears can finally get home with four rushers.

“We’ve got a lot of bullets,” linebacker T.J. Edwards said. “When you can go get them with four, especially with the monster we’ve got there, we needed that. You could feel it. That rush was moving.”

Coach Ben Johnson stressed that he’s focused only on what’s right in front of his team: currently a short week to prepare for the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

“We didn’t come here to make a statement,” he said. “We’re still building and this is part of that process right now and we’ve got a lot of really good pieces. Guys are owning up to their roles, and every little way they can impact this game in a positive fashion, they’re looking to do that.”

The Bears actually have made a couple of statements. They served notice they’re loading up when they traded for Simmons. And they let the NFC, at minimum, know they’re good and getting better just a week after this Seattle team absolutely throttled Patrick Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs.

“We’re a damn good football team,” safety Cam Lewis said. “We’re not a complete team yet. We’re still growing week in and week out. But we’ve got the guys. We’ve got the pieces. We’re just trying to keep getting better week in and week out.

“We don’t want to peak too early. We’ve still got two months left until the playoffs. As long as we keep getting better week in, week out, that’s the way to go.”

They’re a more complete team with Simmons on board.

Williams zipped past Mitch Trubisky (8,554 yards in 2017-2019) as he completed 24 of 34 passes for 247 yards and one touchdown. Williams is at 8,750 yards and counting, but low-hanging Bears passing records aren’t the point.

It was another very efficient game from Williams, his third straight, and he’s playing at a high level since returning from a three-game absence due to a hamstring injury. He completed 76 of 103 passes (73.8%) in victories over the Falcons, Patriots and Seahawks, and his 247-yard effort Monday was notable.

The Seahawks had throttled pretty much every quarterback they had faced this season, with no opponent reaching 200 yards. Williams would have had 286 if a 39-yard screen throw to Kalif Raymond wasn’t ruled a backward delivery, so it counted in rushing statistics.

Williams was crisp from the outset as the Bears set the tone. After the Seahawks opened the game with a three-and-punt, the Bears went on a 17-play, 80-yard drive that ended with a short toss from Williams to Luther Burden III for a 1-yard touchdown.

“I didn’t know it was 17 plays,” coach Ben Johnson said. “Looking back at it, we thought it was going to be tough to get this thing going.”

The Bears watched the Chiefs get nothing going in Seattle last week. They saw the tape on which Kansas City running back Kenneth Walker III, the ex-Seahawk, simply didn’t have daylight on his runs. Would it look that way for them?

“We talked about being patient and if the running game (was) getting 1s, 2s and 3s, we thought we could eventually get to the point where those would turn into 3s, 4s and 5s,” Johnson said. “It’s an outstanding front, a really good scheme. They make it very challenging on you, and we had some really good communication.

“Garrett Bradbury did a nice job driving that train for us. (D’Andre Swift) ran super hard. I know he didn’t have a ton of yards (69), but 27 attempts and three touchdowns, every single yard was earned by him. Those are hard yards to come by.

“Caleb did a great job throughout the game, certainly on that first drive. He took care of the football and he did a lot of really good things throughout.”

‘We don’t waver’: Chicago Bears overcome offensive missteps with big plays by Kalif Raymond and D’Andre Swift

Williams’ vastly improved completion percentage is the first difference from 2025. The numbers match what you’re seeing. The other thing the eye test reveals is he’s doing a better job of letting the game come to him. There aren’t as many situations where it looks like he’s forcing things, and this was the place — a super-loud road stadium — and the opponent where that could have happened quickly in the past.

He did a really good job of taking the underneath throws versus zone coverage, which the Bears had to do. Williams threw a lot of in-breakers, attacking the intermediate void in the field by using Rome Odunze, Colston Loveland and Burden. And he made a couple of plays outside of structure. He really managed the game. He was taking the throws that were there for an offense that again had volume but not a ton of yardage from the ground attack.

“This was one of the more elaborate game plans in terms of what we were asking him to do,” Johnson said. “That had a lot to do with their scheme, and we needed that out of him to make sure we were getting into a good play that had a chance.

“You still look down, you had a couple of delay of games and false starts and things of that nature, so the crowd did impact our operation. But he stayed calm, cool, and collected throughout. There are times where it can get a little bit chaotic, yet he didn’t allow that to faze him at all.”

Johnson said the trust continues to expand, midway through his second season working with Williams. Without that, it’s hard for the play caller-QB relationship to flourish.

“I know if things don’t look great necessarily early in the week, I trust him at this point to get it down by the time we get to game day,” Johnson said. “That’s a credit to his approach right now. It’s awesome. He does a phenomenal job working. I looked out there — I think it was Saturday afternoon after our red-zone practice — and he and (quarterbacks coach) J.T. Barrett are still on the field for an extra hour after practice has already ended.

“That’s where he is right now as a player. He loves downloading all this and bringing it to life on game day. He’s played really well through these last three games.”

From the sound of things, it was as satisfying a midseason win as Williams has experienced.

“That’s who we want to be known as,” he said. “When we come in, we’re also a force to be reckoned with. I mean, they just won the Super Bowl last year. They got a bunch of guys back. That’s a worthy opponent on all sides of the ball: offense, defense, special teams. They got All-Pro guys. They got a bunch of talent over there.

“They got the scheme and so we knew it was going to be a challenge. We knew it was going to be a dogfight. We knew that our identity had to show up for us, and I think it did today.”

The Seahawks struggled to put together consistent drives, but when Bears tight end Colston Loveland had the ball stripped by DeMarcus Lawrence for a turnover that set up Seattle on the Bears 25-yard line, things got a little tense.

Sam Darnold connected with Cooper Kupp four plays later for a 7-yard touchdown and with Tory Horton for a 2-point conversion, and all of a sudden a comfortable Bears cushion turned into a 20-17 lead with 11:46 remaining.

The Bears had third-and-4 on the Seattle 39 when Caleb Williams handed off to D’Andre Swift for a 3-yard loss. Those 3 yards might have pushed them out of kicker Cairo Santos’ range. But officials ruled the ball wasn’t snapped before the play clock expired.

On the subsequent third-and-9, there was confusion as the offense tried to get the play off. Kalif Raymond switched sides of the formation — going from the left to the right. There was some back-and-forth, and then time stopped as Seahawks coach Mike Macdonald wanted to confirm the penalty after it looked like his defense had stopped the Bears. That extra time while referee Shawn Smith was at the sideline proved beneficial.

“Luckily we got delay of game because I ended up messing up a little bit and it allowed us more time to be able to fix it,” Williams said. “Crowd was loud at that point and I missed a word. We got the delay of game and then it allowed us to have a little bit more time because the refs were figuring something out.”

Just like the Bears hit the Patriots a week earlier with a big gain on a wide receiver screen to Luther Burden III, they dialed up another one. This time, Raymond was the target. Rome Odunze got out to block cornerback Josh Jobe, right tackle Darnell Wright got a piece of safety Nick Emmanwori in space and Loveland came across the field to block two defensive backs at once. Raymond was sprung for a 39-yard gain.

“There was a little bit of consternation in there,” Raymond said of the presnap confusion. “We were trying to get in the right alignment, the right formation with what everyone was doing. We ended up getting it right.

“That was a big block by Rome because the guy was pressed on me.”

Swift scored on a 5-yard run on the next play, and just like that the Bears went from potentially punting with a three-point lead to being ahead 27-17. They’ve been pretty resilient through the first eight games, save for the Week 5 trip to Green Bay. When things have turned on them — and there are moments like that in nearly every NFL game — they’ve found solutions and usually quickly.

“When the pressure is high, we want to be at our best,” Ben Johnson said. “You find out more about your identity as a team when you get put in those situations. You talk about it as much as you want and yet to go through it, to live it and to see us come out of the other side, that’s good for building our team.”

For the minority concerned about the exorbitant price — the Bears traded first-round picks in 2027 and 2028 and a 2027 fourth-rounder to the Tennessee Titans for Simmons and a 2028 fifth-round pick — I have an idea to make them feel better.

Root for Poles to make another move before the Nov. 10 trade deadline.

Maybe that sounds counterintuitive to folks worried about how the Bears are going to supply their roster with high-end talent in the next couple of years, and there will be a host of needs on defense alone.

Elite players in their prime — Simmons is 29 and had a career-best 11 sacks last season — aren’t available on the cheap. The Titans did the heavy lifting for the Bears, too, signing Simmons to an extension in June that has him under contract through 2030. As part of that, the Titans already paid him a $20 million signing bonus.

If the ends (winning a Super Bowl or at least reaching one) need to justify the means (raiding future draft capital), why not make an additional move?

Column: Are Chicago Bears ‘all-in’ with Jeffery Simmons deal? Ryan Poles sees it as boon now — and in future.

Predictably, Poles was calculated when asked Friday if there might be another move or moves.

“We’ve got to be very smart about how we move forward when you make a deal like that,” he said. “We’re not just going to throw picks all over the place right now. Obviously we’re going to listen and see if something makes sense or not, but I like to think that whole process will slow down just a little bit.”

Two areas are interesting: edge rusher and cornerback.

First, let’s explore edge rusher.

Entering Week 8, the Los Angeles Chargers had told teams they weren’t selling despite a 0-6 start, with coach Jim Harbaugh apparently dead set on turning a minor (major?) setback into a major comeback.

That didn’t go so well Sunday. The Chargers bolted out to a 9-3 lead against the Los Angeles Rams only to lose 24-9. Harbaugh’s team hasn’t scored an offensive touchdown in the last two games and is one of the huge disappointments of this season.

Are the Chargers, now 0-7 and hosting the Houston Texans (coming off a bye) this week, ready to consider selling? If so, Khalil Mack is worth considering. He had two tackles in a season-low 35 snaps Sunday. Mack has three sacks, five tackles for a loss and six QB hits on the season.

Bears fans have romanticized Mack’s four-year tenure in Chicago a little bit. The team was 29-26 in the 55 games he played in, postseason included. Mack was fantastic in his first season in 2018. He had a sack and an interception return for a touchdown in the season opener and totaled five sacks in the first four games. He was every bit the elite player former GM Ryan Pace figured he was getting, a dynamic chess piece for defensive coordinator Vic Fangio.

Instances of Mack taking over games faded the next two seasons, and a foot injury ended his 2021 season after four games. When Poles came in, the Bears had a tight salary-cap situation, and trading Mack to the Chargers was one of the first moves he made. The only way you can say the Bears won the 2018 trade for Mack is to say the Raiders blew the draft picks they received in the deal.

Mack is 35 and in his 13th season. He has an $8 million base salary on a one-year contract, so the Bears would be picking up about half that, something they could create room for with a little juggling. If the price is right, why not make it clear to the Chargers that if they change their mind about selling, the Bears are interested?

Mack isn’t the same player he was when his Bears stint began, but you can argue he would be an upgrade over any defensive end on the current roster. Here’s another thing that would compel me about Mack: He strikes me as a guy who feeds off the spotlight, something that has been fleeting for him during large stretches of a career spent with the Raiders and an up-and-down Chargers organization. Drop him into the middle of the NFC North race, and I think the Bears could squeeze every bit of remaining production he has to offer.

Everything is fluid. A team that wasn’t a seller one week might be one the next. The Tampa Bay Buccaneers, who under long-tenured GM Jason Licht rarely have been sellers at the trade deadline, looked like they were headed in that direction. Then Baker Mayfield returned from a right thumb injury, and the Bucs stormed into Charlotte and throttled the Carolina Panthers 43-13 on Oct. 25 for their second win of the season. They followed that up by shutting out the Atlanta Falcons 16-0 in the rain Sunday in Tampa.

The Bucs (3-5) have gone from a team that folks around the league had circled as a potential seller to maybe the team to beat in the watered-down NFC South.

First the Bears must quickly evaluate their own roster with Simmons in the mix and a small sample size to consider. Is he a force multiplier for guys like Montez Sweat, his college teammate at Mississippi State? If Simmons’ arrival flips a switch for the mercurial Sweat, maybe the Bears don’t need to deal for an edge rusher.

The Bears sacked Sam Darnold three times Monday night with six QB hits. Sweat had one of the sacks and half of the QB hits, an awakening of sorts for him.

“It’s been a minute since I’ve been able to get to the QB,” said Sweat, who last had a sack in Week 3 and just returned from a two-game PED suspension. “Just getting back around felt great.”

Fellow defensive end Austin Booker was active as well, and his pass deflection turned into James Lynch’s interception. It was a nice showing against a Seattle offensive line that was missing left tackle Charles Cross.

Certainly the Bears will weigh all factors, and maybe Simmons is the multiplier that makes the existing edge rushers viable.

It’s highly unlikely Ryan Poles would unload any more premium draft capital, but Woolen, the rangy Philadelphia Eagles cornerback, could be available and wouldn’t cost too much as a player on a one-year contract. But I have no idea how the Bears feel about him.

Everyone collects cornerbacks. Since Week 1, the Bears have signed four to their practice squad, most recently former Dallas Cowboy Josh Butler, who was plucked from the practice squad of the CFL’s Ottawa Redblacks after spending only four days with them. Cornerbacks are always in demand, and good ones don’t come cheap.

Jaylon Johnson and Tyrique Stevenson Sr. have had well-publicized struggles through the first two months. Malik Muhammad II has flashed but also has had some rookie moments.

The entire secondary had an up-and-down game against the Seahawks, and Muhammad was inactive with a toe injury. Four defensive backs were called for penalties: Johnson, Stevenson, Kyler Gordon and Clark Phillips III. But you have to be grabby at times going against Jaxon Smith-Njigba.

Stevenson had one inexcusable play late in the second quarter. The Seahawks faced third-and-10 at the Bears 43-yard line with 37 seconds until halftime. Stevenson bit on a double move by Smith-Njigba and a five-man pressure didn’t get home, which led to one of Sam Darnold’s few easy throws all night for a 43-yard touchdown. It was the only third down Seattle converted.

“What do you want me to say?” Stevenson said. “You watched it just like me. It’s a double move.”

Smith-Njigba finished with six receptions in 11 targets for 118 yards, but he never took over the game. He caught screen passes that went for 21 and 16 yards in a span of three snaps on Seattle’s second possession. The second one the Bears weren’t prepared for, as Seattle had two-on-one against Stevenson on the outside. Stevenson signaled for help before the snap, but it didn’t arrive until a big play had happened.

So 85 of Smith-Njigba’s yards came on the two screens and the busted coverage on the double move. Stevenson drew an offensive pass interference penalty against Smith-Njigba on one occasion.

“We did our job,” Stevenson said. “We knew he was going to get the ball force-fed to him. Best thing to do is contain him. On that double move I didn’t contain him as much as we should.

“He’s a great receiver, one of the best in the league. He can win the game by himself. Our goal was to come in here and not let him do that, and he didn’t.”

Darnold’s other touchdown pass went to Cooper Kupp when Stevenson was in coverage.

When I asked Poles on Friday how he evaluated the outside cornerbacks, he mentioned how the addition of Jeffery Simmons should affect the entire defense.

“Going back to Jeffery, I think he’s a multiplier,” Poles said. “When you can provide pressure, you help your secondary tremendously. (Ben Johnson) hit on it: I think secondary-wise, it’s been some ups and downs. I love what I’ve seen Kyler (Gordon) do in certain situations. I’ve really liked Malik, his maturity. There’s been ups and downs for him, too, but he’s a young player.

“And then same with Jaylon and Tyrique. There’s been ups and downs and they’re trying to find their way. But I do think when you add someone like Jeffery, you make a huge impact for them too.”

Some have wondered if the Bears could get Nahshon Wright back from the New York Jets. Wright was inactive for Sunday’s loss to the Raiders and has appeared in only three games with zero snaps on defense. Surely he could be had for cheap, maybe in some sort of late-round pick swap.

The market told you what the league thought of Wright after his eye-opening season for the Bears last year, when he had five interceptions after being reunited with secondary coach Al Harris. The Jets got him in free agency for $3.5 million with $2 million in incentives that he’s unlikely to reach.

The Bears didn’t have a ton of cap flexibility in March, but surely they could have matched that deal or maybe even done a little better if they had been motivated to keep Wright. According to Pro Football Reference, quarterbacks had an 86.5 passer rating when targeting Wright in 2025. That’s with the five interceptions, and that’s because there was a lot of production when Wright wasn’t getting his hands on the ball. The 805 passing yards Wright allowed, per PFR, was the fourth-highest figure in the league.

I’m not saying the idea of bringing back Wright is a bad one — at least for a little depth — but I’m offering a reminder that the takeaways and 11 pass breakups he had last year made it easy for folks to forget there were many big plays that went against him.

There has been speculation the Eagles might trade Woolen, who signed a one-year contract with them this season. The Eagles are in disarray and will be one of the fascinating teams to watch over the next week because GM Howie Roseman is a shrewd operator.

Woolen is a thicker version of Wright — a very tall outside cornerback at 6-foot-4. He had six interceptions as a rookie for the Seahawks in 2022. Since then, there might not be a cornerback in the league who has had a greater range of play from impressive to at times not good. The Seahawks have been pretty sharp in building their team, and Woolen’s role was diminished last season before he wasn’t re-signed.

One thing Woolen would add for the Bears is speed. He can absolutely fly, but he has inconsistent eye discipline and his tackling can be up and down as well.

Starting-caliber cornerbacks don’t come cheap. If they’re available, there’s probably a reason. Maybe the Bears can identify another option at the position that makes sense, but it seems unlikely there’s a deal at a reasonable price for a cornerback who would come in and be an immediate starting upgrade.

It has been clear for some time that cornerback will be among the Bears’ top two needs in the next offseason. Currently, it’s not in second place.

Of late, a dominant defensive tackle also is required to win a Super Bowl. That reality wasn’t lost on the Bears as they considered the move to add Jeffery Simmons.

Each of the last seven Super Bowl champions has had one or more elite interior defenders. Is that a trend to look at moving forward, or more of a coincidence, considering most Super Bowl champions have a lot of very good players at a lot of positions? Who knows. But check out the monsters in the middle for the previous seven Lombardi Trophy winners:

For as much hollering and hand-wringing as there was at the start of this offseason about the Bears edge rushers, I thought defensive tackle was an even greater need. Here’s what I wrote coming out of the scouting combine in Indianapolis on Feb. 27:

“You can make a strong case that defensive tackle is the No. 1 need for 2026. That’s based on the current projected depth chart and without considering what will be available in free agency and the draft. Defensive end has gotten more attention because it’s clear to everyone the pass rush needs to be ramped up, and edge rusher is the first position you think about when talking about the pass rush.”

The Bears made a series of moves on the interior by signing some second-wave free agents. None moves the needle like Simmons, whose career track record puts him in a class with the group of Super Bowl winners listed above.

A disruptive factor in the middle of the defense means a ton. It’s why Akiem Hicks, in his prime, was so valuable for the Bears. Hicks had a monster three-season period from 2016-18 in which he had 23 sacks, 38 tackles for a loss, 53 QB hits and five forced fumbles. Injuries and a lack of surrounding talent made Hicks less impactful in his final three seasons with the Bears, but that three-year stretch was elite play that deserved more recognition than one Pro Bowl nod.

A defense has to be able to win on the edges, but a defensive tackle gets better pass-rushing matchups inside versus guards. You can expose guards who are weak in pass protection. You can do a lot of twisting and stunting inside that gets the tackles a better path to the quarterback.

Defensive tackles who are considered “blues” (top-tier players) affect the quarterback at a high rate because they’re in the middle of the field and they’re at the quarterback’s feet a lot quicker. Look at the quarterbacks in the NFC North. If you can take away Jared Goff’s ability to step up in the pocket for the Lions, that’s a huge thing. Why did the Bears invest so heavily in the interior of their offensive line when Ben Johnson arrived? He wanted to create a strong pocket for Caleb Williams.

There will be hyperfocus on Simmons’ individual production throughout the remainder of the season, and that comes with the territory when you’re the league’s second-highest-paid player at your position.

The Bears want Simmons to make a strength they’ve had this season stronger. They’ve been at their best on third down and they want to accentuate that. Entering Monday night, the Bears defense was No. 1 in the league on third down at 26.1%, with the Seahawks (27.9%) and Vikings (29.7%) right behind them.

Dennis Allen’s defense, if it can get to even third-and-medium distance, has been lights out. Entering Monday, opponents were converting 16.3% on third-and-5 or longer. They were 2-for-24 (8.3%) on third-and-10 or longer.

That’s what the Bears are hunting on defense, especially with takeaways not coming in bunches as they did in 2025, and Monday’s game was an Allen master class. The Seahawks were 1-for-11 on third down. There was one third-and-4 — it happened with 2:25 remaining and the game decided — and two third-and-5s. Everything else was third-and-7 or longer.

The Bears dominated third down because they won on first and second down, limiting running backs Zach Charbonnet and Jadarian Price to 52 yards on 16 carries combined.

Allen can really disguise what he wants to do on third down. The recent return of nickel cornerback Kyler Gordon provided flexibility, and Simmons brings even more. Allen can count on disrupting the quarterback with only four rushers with some level of confidence now. That has been very difficult for the Bears to do.

Entering Week 12 last season, the Bears were No. 2 in the league on third down at 33.7% and had been doing a really nice job of getting off the field. Then it all caved in on Allen’s unit. Opponents converted 43 of 87 third downs (49.4%) over the final seven regular-season games, and the defense finished the season ranked 22nd at 40.8%.

It’s going to be a challenge for the Bears to finish the season first in the league on third down, especially considering some of the offenses they will encounter after the bye week. But this was an eye-opening performance that expanded their lead. Simmons gives them a chance, and his presence ought to prevent a repeat collapse.

In the postseason, who knows? Of late, the champions have all had a guy like Simmons in the middle.

Jackson has a right thumb injury that will require surgery and could sideline him for the remainder of the season, and Huntley exited with a turf toe injury. That left the Ravens with Joe Fagnano, an undrafted rookie who played his college ball at Connecticut and Maine. But Fagnano has an ankle injury, and the Ravens on Monday signed former Bears quarterback Austin Reed to their practice squad.

The Ravens host the Jacksonville Jaguars on Thursday night, so it’s probably too late to find a starter other than Fagnano for that game. But plenty of folks are connecting the dots between Ravens offensive coordinator Declan Doyle and Bears quarterback Tyson Bagent.

It’s interesting to consider the Bears as a potential seller as well, but are the Ravens really in a spot where they’re going to make a big move? They’re in last place in the AFC North at 4-4 and they’ve lost three consecutive games.

Let’s say the Jaguars (an 8½-point favorite) win Thursday. That would drop the Ravens to 4-5. In that scenario, there would be four AFC teams with six wins, a group that doesn’t include Patrick Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs (5-2).

Is Ravens GM Eric DeCosta, who already made a sizable in-season trade for center Cam Jurgens, going to deal quality draft assets for a quarterback who — maybe with a lot of help around him — can keep the flicker of hope alive for a deep playoff run? Without knowing how long Huntley potentially will be sidelined, that seems a little far-fetched.

Would the Bears consider trading Bagent? Of course he’d be available. Last week’s acquisition of Jeffery Simmons is a well-timed reminder that nearly every player in the league has a price.

Bagent, who is 3-3 as a starter if you overlook the oddball beginning of the Week 4 win over the Jets, remained the No. 2 quarterback for Ben Johnson even after the dud the following week in Green Bay. Bagent got pulled for Case Keenum in the second half of the 31-7 loss to the Packers, but that didn’t alter the depth chart. Keenum remained the emergency No. 3 quarterback when Caleb Williams returned.

Johnson still believes in Bagent and has talked at length for a year and a half about how strong the dynamic is in that room and how beneficial that is for Williams. Would Johnson sign off on altering the chemistry of the group? For the right price, why not?

Bagent would be able to step in and pick up Doyle’s playbook quickly. No question about that.  This strikes me as a pivotal and perhaps franchise-altering moment for the Ravens. Jackson, who already missed three games this season with an ankle injury, has a cap figure of $84 million in 2027. If this injury is season-ending, it’s possible he has played his final game for Baltimore. The Ravens will have to work out a new deal for Jackson, who missed four games last season, or chart a new course.

No one understands the magnitude of the situation better than DeCosta. With the possibility that the Ravens will be looking for a new quarterback come the offseason, are they going to make a considerable move for first-year coach Jesse Minter? That’s the kind of rash move the franchise has largely avoided for the past couple of decades.

If someone believes Bagent can give them a chance, he’s attractive from the standpoint that he’s under contract in 2027 for $5 million. The Doyle connection makes it worthy of discussion, for sure. But it’s quite possible the Bears value Bagent more than any of the other 31 teams.

A quarterback situation that’s maybe more compelling is what’s happening in Minnesota. Kyler Murray has struggled, and with the Vikings losing for the first time Sunday in Detroit, would they potentially shop for a replacement?

That was my unofficial count, and Ben Johnson said after the game he would have to see the film. But the Bears didn’t shy away from their personnel packages with multiple tight ends.

Of the 70 offensive plays, I tallied 39 in 11 personnel (one running back, three wide receivers, one tight end), 21 in 12 personnel (one back, two receivers, two tight ends) and 11 in 13 personnel (one back, one receiver, three tight ends). They were in 13 for the final four snaps.

Roush was candidly harsh about his play and mistakes earlier in the season but feels like he has been more consistent for three weeks now, if not a little longer. Tight ends coach Jim Dray singled out a block Roush had in short yardage the previous week against the Patriots when Roush waited for a defensive end to cross his face and then got two-for-one, taking out two defenders because he had patience on the play.

“Confidence couldn’t be higher,” Dray said of Roush. “That’s why he is here and that’s why they’re trained a certain way. He’s expected to go out there and win his one-on-one matchups.

“I don’t know what rookie doesn’t go through rookie struggles. He is gaining more confidence at this level and this is a tough position to play at this level. We ask those guys to do a lot. He still has a long way to go but he’s on the right track.”

The Bears also promoted veteran Stephen Carlson, 29, from the practice squad and could do that again for a couple of games. He has been with the team since 2023, and Dray called him a “trusted agent.”

Kmet suffered a right knee injury late in the Oct. 22 win over the Patriots. The specifics of the injury are unknown, but Dr. Neal ElAttrache performed surgery on Kmet in Los Angeles and the rehabilitation process has begun.

It’s a setback for the Bears and not just because Kmet was dependable in whatever role he was needed on the field. He’s a player coaches could turn to in order to take the pulse of the locker room. Kmet didn’t have a “C” on his jersey as a captain, but he was one in every sense of the role.

How do the Chicago Bears move on without TE Cole Kmet? ‘I don’t see us really changing who we are.’

“He’s one of our most consistent leaders and one of our most consistent players,” offensive coordinator Press Taylor said. “Whenever we break down certain periods, he’s the first guy we’re looking at. Everyone is looking at Cole. He’s one of the most experienced. Understands what it takes to be a good player. Productive. The most well-prepared. He is a problem solver for us. It’s tough.”

Kmet was the first player GM Ryan Poles signed to an extension. He was drafted by the previous regime, but Poles signed Kmet to a new deal in July 2023, so there’s a bond there as well.

“It’s a big loss for us, not just on the field but also off the field and what he meant to us,” Poles said. “He’s such a stable, dependable  … player and human being. He means a lot to us.

“Our focus now is what I told Kyle (McCarthy), his agent. Our return-to-play process and what we surround our guys with to get them back to their original form and being confident as a football player I feel like is elite. We’re going to continue to do that. We’re going to surround Cole and put him in a position where it’s going to be a long journey, for sure, but when he comes back, he’s going to be the best version of himself. We’re going to surround him and make sure he’s got everything he needs to get back to what he was.”

Kmet, 27, is signed for 2027 at $10 million with a $15.4 million cap hit. He has a $1 million roster bonus due on the fifth day of the league year. It’s premature to speculate how things could shake out.

The Colts dealt eight-time Pro Bowl guard Quenton Nelson and three-time Pro Bowl defensive tackle DeForest Buckner as they dived headfirst into an accelerated rebuild — just a year after they were an aggressive buyer at the deadline in acquiring cornerback Sauce Gardner from the Jets.

Nelson went to the Seahawks, who made a bid to stabilize the interior of their offensive line, in exchange for a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-rounder. ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler reported that the Bears were one of a couple of other teams that had varying levels of interest.

How deep the Bears got into discussions about possibly adding Nelson, I don’t know, but Fowler’s report was accurate. This is a great reminder that there’s constant dialogue going on in the front office and “what if” conversations are the norm.

It’s fascinating because interior offensive line is about the last position most would figure the Bears were considering. Right guard Jonah Jackson had a left hip injury in Week 6 in Atlanta but rebounded on a short week to play against the New England Patriots and wasn’t on the injury report leading into Monday’s game.

Why would the Bears have been sniffing around Nelson while also considering defensive pieces that could aid them for the second half of the season? Perhaps it’s as simple as when a player with Nelson’s credentials becomes available — no matter the position — it’s worth a discussion.

The first thing that came to mind was maybe the Bears were trying to prevent Nelson from heading to a team they might have to beat to reach the Super Bowl. The Packers, who have had an assortment of injuries on their offensive line, come to mind. Fowler reported the Packers were another team in the mix — at some level — for Nelson. The Seahawks, of course, were in that mix as well.

In a scenario in which the Bears had acquired Nelson, he would have been an instant starter for them. He started at left guard for all 136 games he played for the Colts. He did take eight snaps at left tackle during a Week 14 game in 2020 in Las Vegas.

My hunch is the Bears would have slotted in Nelson at left guard and shifted Joe Thuney to left tackle. In the end, nothing happened and the Bears went shopping for an even bigger target in Jeffery Simmons.

Ozzy Trapilo had a few rough snaps against the Patriots when he subbed in for Benedet, especially in pass protection. Trapilo made a tremendous recovery from a torn patellar tendon, but he also has missed a lot of practice time.

“The idea has been, ‘Hey, let’s keep getting Ozzy ready for if that time comes (when he’s needed),'” offensive line coach Dan Roushar said last week. “That’s No. 1.”

I asked Roushar if they are expecting bumps in the road for Trapilo again because of the long layoff.

“You are, but you don’t go in with the anticipation that he’s going to struggle,” Roushar said. “You go in feeling like there is still rust to be knocked off.”

They still feel good about Trapilo, and we’ll probably see him in the mix in some capacity again soon. Luke Newman was the tackle eligible for jumbo sets in Monday’s game.

10a. When Ben Johnson says he’s legitimately focused from week to week on players, I believe him. But I also think he fielded a good question Saturday when he was asked if there’s a possibility the Bears will wait until after the bye week to bring back running back Kyle Monangai.

“I can’t speak to that,” Johnson said. “I don’t see him playing (in Seattle). I’m hopeful every week, though, that he’ll make his return because he knows how much we want him here on offense and he can give a spark.”

A turf toe injury suffered in the Oct. 4 win over the Jets, in which Monangai carried 30 times for 146 yards and two touchdowns, has sidelined him for four games. Monangai has yet to see the practice field, and now the Bears are on a short week. They’ll hold a walk-through late Wednesday, and I’m curious what the Thursday schedule will look like.

I’m skeptical they would have Monangai back for two practices — max — after missing a month and then add him to the mix Sunday night against the Buccaneers. Maybe Monangai can get some light work at the end of this week and aim for a return Nov. 22 versus the New Orleans Saints at Soldier Field.

Everyone knows how valuable Monangai is to the offense and rushing attack, and the Bears need him for the stretch run. Some extra time with the bye on the other end of the Bucs game might make the most sense at this point.

10b. D’Andre Swift’s three rushing touchdowns propelled him to the top of the NFL with 10. Bills quarterback Josh Allen is next with nine, and five running backs have eight touchdowns.

Swift is the first Bears player to rush for 10 or more touchdowns in the first eight games since Rick Casares in 1956. Neal Anderson had nine through eight games in 1990.

But let’s talk about 10 rushing touchdowns in a full season for a Bears running back. You have to go all the way back to Raymont Harris in 1997 for the last time that happened. Rashaan Salaam had 10 in 1995. Anderson accomplished the feat three times after Walter Payton had five such seasons. It has been a long time.

10c. In researching big-time in-season trades that paid off for teams, the first one that came to mind was the Los Angeles Rams’ 2021 trade to acquire edge rusher Von Miller from the Denver Broncos for second- and third-round picks.

Rams GM Les Snead has been as aggressive as anyone when it comes to flipping draft picks for proven players, and Miller stepped up in a major way down the stretch that season with five sacks in the final four games. He had two more sacks in the playoffs and then two in a comeback victory over the Cincinnati Bengals in Super Bowl LVI.

But no in-season acquisition was more impactful than Fred Dean was for the San Francisco 49ers in 1981. The Niners sent the San Diego Chargers a second-round pick for Dean, and he produced 12 sacks (the year before it became an official statistic) in 11 regular-season games. San Francisco won the Super Bowl that season and captured another with Dean leading the defense before his Hall of Fame career ended.

10d. Not to look too far ahead, but the Bears are scheduled to play in Seattle again in the 2027 regular season. They will be heading west for four games with trips to Denver, Las Vegas and Los Angeles (Rams).

10e. The Bears opened as a six-point favorite over the Buccaneers at Circa Sports for Sunday night’s game at Soldier Field.
